screens.title: What is a Multi-Account Strategy?
screens.narratorSegment: A multi-account strategy is the practice of organizing workloads and environments into separate AWS accounts to create strong isolation boundaries and clearer governance. That means instead of one account for everything, you deliberately partition functions: a management account to run AWS Organizations and billing, a log archive account for immutable audit data, a security account for tooling, shared services for cross-account resources, and separate dev/test and production accounts. The key benefits are reduced blast radius for security incidents, simplified compliance because you can apply specific policies to groups of accounts, and improved cost management through consolidated billing and per-account cost visibility. For example, if a developer accidentally creates large ephemeral resources in a dev account, the impact stays local to that account and billing reports can show chargebacks to the right team. A common misconception is to think a multi-account approach complicates operations; while it adds some cross-account configuration work, the operational clarity, isolation, and faster incident triage you gain usually outweigh the overhead. When you design a topology, ask: which data must be kept immutable, which services must be central, and where do teams need autonomy? That framing guides sensible account boundaries.

screens.title: Core components of AWS Organizations
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Organizations gives you a hierarchical control plane to manage many accounts at scale. The organization is the top-level container for all member accounts. Within it, the Root is the default, parent container where you can view the entire account tree and start creating Organizational Units, or OUs. OUs are logical groupings for accounts used to apply policies together — for instance grouping all development accounts under a Development OU and all production accounts under Production OU. Member accounts live inside these OUs and retain their own IAM users, roles, and resources, but they inherit organization-level guardrails from attached Service Control Policies. Think of the Organization as the administrative envelope and OUs as folders inside it that let you apply consistent governance. A common mistake is applying broad-deny SCPs at the Root without testing in a lower-scope OU — this can inadvertently block organization administrators. When designing, map each account to a function, and then map OUs to policy domains such as environment, regulatory scope, or business unit. This architecture supports clear policy delegation and reduces the risk of ad-hoc account sprawl.

Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › AWS Organizations
Hierarchy and responsibility
The organization is the administrative boundary. Inside it, the Root contains OUs that group accounts by policy scope or environment.
Organizational Unit (OU)
Group accounts for consistent policy application, for example Development OU vs Production OU.
Member Account
Holds resources and IAM principals. Policies from OUs and Root limit what can be done here.
Service Control Policy (SCP)
Attach to Root, OU, or account to restrict the maximum permissions allowed in affected accounts.
Annotated example
Root
Top-level container. Attach org-wide SCPs here only when confident about impacts.
Development OU
Less-restrictive SCPs to allow rapid experimentation but with region controls.
Misconfiguration risk
Applying a deny widely without scoped testing can block administrators and automation workflows.

screens.title: Service Control Policies (SCPs)
screens.narratorSegment: Service Control Policies are organization-level JSON policies you attach to the Root, an OU, or an individual account. Their purpose is to define the maximum available permissions for IAM principals in the affected accounts. Importantly, SCPs do not grant permissions; they only restrict the set of actions that IAM policies and roles can allow. For example, an SCP can explicitly deny deletion of CloudTrail trails across accounts or deny creation of resources outside a chosen region. A common practical pattern is to use SCPs to enforce compliance boundaries — deny actions that would violate policy — while continuing to manage more granular permissions via IAM inside each account. A typical misconception is treating SCPs like IAM policies; they are different layers: an IAM policy grants or denies within an account scope, an SCP narrows the maximum allowed actions regardless of IAM grants. When you design SCPs, test them in a development OU before applying them to production, and include logging to ensure the deny behavior is observed. Ask: which destructive actions must be impossible anywhere in the organization? Service Control Policies (SCPs) means scps set maximum permissions and only restrict actions. use them as guardrails, not as a grant mechanism.. In practical terms, how scps act as guardrails and a clear example of restrictive policy behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Service Control Policies
SCPs as guardrails

SCPs narrow the maximum permissions available to IAM principals in member accounts. They are applied at organization nodes and evaluated before IAM policies.

Behavior
SCPs do not grant permissions. They only deny or allow at the org boundary.
Example use
Prevent deletion of critical logs or prevent resource creation in disallowed regions.
Pitfall
Applying broad denies at Root without testing can block needed operations for admins and automation.
Concrete scenario
You want to ensure no account can delete CloudTrail trails. Create an SCP that denies cloudtrail:DeleteTrail and attach it to the logging OU. Even users with administrator IAM policies in the logging account will be blocked by this SCP.
Key takeaway

Treat SCPs as organization-level safety nets. Define denies for non-negotiable actions and test before broad deployment.

screens.title: Example Service Control Policy (JSON)
screens.narratorSegment: Let's examine a concrete Service Control Policy JSON example that demonstrates common guardrail patterns. The policy denies certain creation actions unless the requested region is in an allowed list, explicitly denies all actions from the root principal, and prevents CloudTrail deletion. This shows three practical techniques: region restrictions to control sprawl, principal-based denies to protect account root, and service-specific denies for audit integrity. When you read the JSON, focus on the Effect field set to Deny and the Condition blocks that narrowly target unwanted behavior. A frequent misunderstanding is to expect this SCP to make an IAM user able to perform actions; it cannot grant rights. Instead, if an IAM policy grants an action but the SCP denies it, the deny wins. When implementing, attach the policy to a Development OU to limit where resource creation is allowed to permitted regions, and then test by attempting the blocked action from a member account to observe an UnauthorizedOperation error. Keep policies targeted and additive where possible to avoid unintended denials. Example Service Control Policy (JSON) means use json scps for region restrictions, root protection, and service-specific denies. remember: denies override iam grants.. In practical terms, sample scp that restricts resource creation to specific regions and denies root access. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › SCP JSON Example
SCP JSON walkthrough

This policy denies run/create actions outside allowed regions, blocks root principal actions, and prevents CloudTrail deletion. It is applied at OU or account level.

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "DenyDisallowedRegions",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": [
        "ec2:RunInstances",
        "s3:CreateBucket",
        "rds:CreateDBInstance"
      ],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "StringNotEquals": {
          "aws:RequestedRegion": [
            "us-east-1",
            "us-west-2"
          ]
        }
      }
    },
    {
      "Sid": "DenyRootUserAccess",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": "*",
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "StringEquals": {
          "aws:PrincipalArn": "arn:aws:iam::*:root"
        }
      }
    },
    {
      "Sid": "DenyCloudTrailDeletion",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": [
        "cloudtrail:DeleteTrail",
        "cloudtrail:StopLogging"
      ],
      "Resource": "*"
    }
  ]
}
Notes & testing
  • Attach to an OU to enforce across multiple accounts.
  • Test in a Development OU before applying to Production.
  • Remember: an SCP deny will cause an UnauthorizedOperation when attempted from a member account.
Pro tip

Include targeted Conditions so denies only apply where needed instead of a blanket deny.

screens.title: Applying an SCP — Steps to Deploy and Test
screens.narratorSegment: Deploying an SCP safely means following a checklist: enable policies, author the policy, attach it to a target, and verify behavior. Start by confirming that AWS Organizations is enabled in the management account. Next, create the SCP JSON in the console or via A P I, keeping conditions and scopes as narrow as possible. Attach the SCP to an OU rather than the Root when testing so you avoid organization-wide impact. Then, create or use a member account in the target OU and attempt the action you expect to be denied, such as creating an instance in a restricted region. Observe the UnauthorizedOperation error to confirm enforcement. Finally, review CloudTrail to see deny events and update the policy if you encounter unintended denials. A common misconception is skipping validation; without testing you may block automation or admin workflows. Always plan a rollback: keep an easier-to-revoke test policy and monitor logs for denied events. The guided sequence reduces risk and helps you iterate on the guardrail until it matches your governance needs. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Step-by-step

Enable AWS Organizations
Confirm from the management account you can create OUs and policies.

Create SCP

screens.title: AWS SSO vs Cross-Account IAM Roles
screens.narratorSegment: Managing identities across many accounts can become a burden if you rely on separate IAM users inside each account. Two common patterns are AWS Single Sign-On and cross-account IAM roles. AWS SSO centralizes access: users sign in once to access multiple accounts with assigned roles, often integrating with corporate directories. This reduces user lifecycle complexity because your identity source is a single place to add or remove access. Cross-account IAM roles are an alternative where one account defines roles that trusted principals from another account can assume. This works well for automation or for a small set of admin users who need to switch into production accounts. A typical trade-off: AWS SSO simplifies human access at scale and reduces administrative overhead, while cross-account roles give fine-grained control for service-to-service or scripted access. A misconception is that cross-account roles eliminate the need for centralized identity; they do not — they are a technique for delegation. In practice, use AWS SSO for human access and cross-account roles for automated workflows where necessary. Ask: which approach reduces manual user management most in your organization?

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › SSO vs Cross-Account Roles
AWS Single Sign-On
Centralizes human user access and role assignments across multiple AWS accounts, often integrating with corporate directories for one-place user lifecycle management.
Why choose SSO
Simplifies onboarding/offboarding, reduces duplicate users, and automates role creation across accounts.
Cross-account IAM roles
A role in one account can be assumed by principals in another account. Useful for automation and trusted delegation between specific accounts.
When to use roles
For automation, scripts, or tightly-scoped admin tasks where SSO is not available.
Misconception

Cross-account roles replace identity centralization. They do not; they delegate privileges and still require careful lifecycle management.

screens.title: Typical Enterprise Multi-Account Layout
screens.narratorSegment: Enterprises commonly adopt a repeatable layout for account roles. At the top, the Management (or Master) account is reserved for AWS Organizations administration and billing; it should not host general workloads. The Log Archive account centralizes CloudTrail logs, Config snapshots, and other immutable audit records and should have very strict access controls. The Security account houses monitoring, SIEM, and detection tooling, plus IAM roles used by the security team. A Shared Services account holds cross-account resources like directories, CI/CD infrastructure, or network endpoints. Then you have Development and Test accounts where teams can experiment with more permissive policies, and Production accounts with stricter SCPs and auditing. screens.title: Console Walkthrough: Create OU and Attach an SCP
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity outlines the console steps to create an Organizational Unit and attach an SCP that restricts resource creation to a single region. First, enable AWS Organizations from the management account if not already enabled. Next, in the Organizations console select the Root, choose Actions, and create a new OU named Development. Then use the Add account flow to create a new DevAccount1 and move it into the Development OU. Create the SCP by navigating to Policies, then Service Control Policies, and author the JSON that denies creation outside the allowed region. Attach the SCP to the Development OU. Finally, log into DevAccount1 via AWS SSO or by assuming the OrganizationAccountAccessRole and attempt to create an EC2 instance in the allowed region to confirm success, then try a disallowed region to observe the UnauthorizedOperation error. screens.title: Consolidated Billing and Cost Visibility
screens.narratorSegment: Consolidated billing allows all accounts within an organization to be paid by a single management account. From an operational perspective this centralizes payment and often obtains volume discounts across accounts. From a governance perspective, consolidated billing improves cost visibility: you can break down spend by account or OU to enable chargebacks or showback to teams. Use tags and account-level reporting to make chargebacks accurate. One common mistake is relying solely on consolidated billing and not implementing per-account budgets or alerts; while billing is centralized, each team still benefits from budget controls in their account to prevent runaway costs. Another practical pattern is to keep sandbox and experiment accounts under strict budget controls and alerts. Finally, ensure that shared services costs are apportioned clearly to consumers, and document the billing ownership model. Ask yourself: how will teams be billed for shared services and who will approve cross-account expenditures? Clear answers avoid disputes and surprise invoices. screens.title: Best Practices and Operational Guidance
screens.narratorSegment: When implementing a multi-account strategy, apply a few consistent best practices. First, reserve the management account strictly for Organizations and billing. Do not run general workloads there; this reduces risk and simplifies recovery. Second, centralize logs and audit data into a hardened Log Archive account and restrict access with SCPs and bucket policies. Third, use OUs to group accounts by policy needs — environment, regulatory boundary, or business unit — and attach SCPs at the OU level for consistent guardrails. Fourth, prefer AWS SSO for human access at scale and use cross-account roles selectively for automation or trusted delegation. Fifth, always test policies in a non-production OU before broad deployment and maintain a rollback path. Common mistakes include over-broad denies at Root, neglecting per-account budgets, and failing to route logs centrally. Finally, document ownership, billing, and incident response responsibilities for each account to avoid confusion during incidents. These practices keep your organization governable as it scales and reduce the chance of surprises. fullNarratorScript:
As your cloud estate grows, treating a single AWS account as a home for everything becomes fragile and risky. In this lesson you will learn why a multi-account strategy is a core architectural pattern: it creates strong isolation boundaries for security, simplifies compliance by grouping similar workloads, and makes cost visibility and chargebacks clear through consolidated billing. We will also explore AWS Organizations — the service that creates an organizational root, lets you build Organizational Units, and apply Service Control Policies as guardrails. You’ll see practical account types commonly used in enterprises: master or management for governance, log archive for immutable audit trails, security for detection and response tooling, shared services for common infra, separate dev/test and production accounts for lifecycle separation, and sandboxes for experimentation. By the end of this chapter you should be able to propose a simple multi-account layout, explain how SCPs restrict actions, and recommend where to centralize billing and logging. Keep in mind a common misconception: policies at the organization level do not grant permissions, they only limit them. Ask yourself: which accounts in your current architecture would benefit most from being separated?

These objectives frame our practical outcomes. First, you will explain why a multi-account strategy improves security, compliance, and cost management. That means being able to describe how isolation reduces blast radius and how separate accounts make auditing and regulatory separation easier. Second, you will describe the core components of AWS Organizations: the organization itself, the root, organizational units, accounts, and Service Control Policies. You’ll be expected to explain what each element does and how they relate. Third, you will implement Service Control Policies to enforce guardrails. This includes writing or applying an SCP that denies specified actions across accounts and testing its effect. Finally on this screen you’ll learn to interpret SCP behavior: SCPs only restrict permissions and do not grant them. Throughout these objectives we use short scenarios to connect decisions with outcomes, so you can design a safer and more maintainable AWS estate.

Continuing our objectives, you will design a basic multi-account structure suitable for many enterprises. This includes selecting account roles such as management, log archive, security, shared services, development, production, and sandbox. You’ll learn why the management account should avoid hosting workloads, why a log archive is a hardened landing zone for audit data, and where to centralize security tooling. Next, you will identify best practices for managing IAM users and roles across accounts using AWS Single Sign-On or with cross-account IAM roles. That means knowing when to use AWS SSO to simplify role assignment and when a purpose-built cross-account role is appropriate. Finally, you will be able to map policy decisions like SCPs to OUs and explain test scenarios to validate policy behavior. Each objective includes short scenarios so you can reason about trade-offs and avoid common pitfalls such as putting workloads in the management account or assuming SCPs grant permissions.

A multi-account strategy is the practice of organizing workloads and environments into separate AWS accounts to create strong isolation boundaries and clearer governance. That means instead of one account for everything, you deliberately partition functions: a management account to run AWS Organizations and billing, a log archive account for immutable audit data, a security account for tooling, shared services for cross-account resources, and separate dev/test and production accounts. The key benefits are reduced blast radius for security incidents, simplified compliance because you can apply specific policies to groups of accounts, and improved cost management through consolidated billing and per-account cost visibility. For example, if a developer accidentally creates large ephemeral resources in a dev account, the impact stays local to that account and billing reports can show chargebacks to the right team. A common misconception is to think a multi-account approach complicates operations; while it adds some cross-account configuration work, the operational clarity, isolation, and faster incident triage you gain usually outweigh the overhead. When you design a topology, ask: which data must be kept immutable, which services must be central, and where do teams need autonomy? That framing guides sensible account boundaries.

AWS Organizations gives you a hierarchical control plane to manage many accounts at scale. The organization is the top-level container for all member accounts. Within it, the Root is the default, parent container where you can view the entire account tree and start creating Organizational Units, or OUs. OUs are logical groupings for accounts used to apply policies together — for instance grouping all development accounts under a Development OU and all production accounts under Production OU. Member accounts live inside these OUs and retain their own IAM users, roles, and resources, but they inherit organization-level guardrails from attached Service Control Policies. Think of the Organization as the administrative envelope and OUs as folders inside it that let you apply consistent governance. A common mistake is applying broad-deny SCPs at the Root without testing in a lower-scope OU — this can inadvertently block organization administrators. When designing, map each account to a function, and then map OUs to policy domains such as environment, regulatory scope, or business unit. This architecture supports clear policy delegation and reduces the risk of ad-hoc account sprawl.

Service Control Policies are organization-level JSON policies you attach to the Root, an OU, or an individual account. Their purpose is to define the maximum available permissions for IAM principals in the affected accounts. Importantly, SCPs do not grant permissions; they only restrict the set of actions that IAM policies and roles can allow. For example, an SCP can explicitly deny deletion of CloudTrail trails across accounts or deny creation of resources outside a chosen region. A common practical pattern is to use SCPs to enforce compliance boundaries — deny actions that would violate policy — while continuing to manage more granular permissions via IAM inside each account. A typical misconception is treating SCPs like IAM policies; they are different layers: an IAM policy grants or denies within an account scope, an SCP narrows the maximum allowed actions regardless of IAM grants. When you design SCPs, test them in a development OU before applying them to production, and include logging to ensure the deny behavior is observed. Ask: which destructive actions must be impossible anywhere in the organization? The policy denies certain creation actions unless the requested region is in an allowed list, explicitly denies all actions from the root principal, and prevents CloudTrail deletion. Consolidated billing allows all accounts within an organization to be paid by a single management account. From an operational perspective this centralizes payment and often obtains volume discounts across accounts. From a governance perspective, consolidated billing improves cost visibility: you can break down spend by account or OU to enable chargebacks or showback to teams. Use tags and account-level reporting to make chargebacks accurate. One common mistake is relying solely on consolidated billing and not implementing per-account budgets or alerts; while billing is centralized, each team still benefits from budget controls in their account to prevent runaway costs. Another practical pattern is to keep sandbox and experiment accounts under strict budget controls and alerts. Finally, ensure that shared services costs are apportioned clearly to consumers, and document the billing ownership model. Ask yourself: how will teams be billed for shared services and who will approve cross-account expenditures? Clear answers avoid disputes and surprise invoices. When implementing a multi-account strategy, apply a few consistent best practices. First, reserve the management account strictly for Organizations and billing. Do not run general workloads there; this reduces risk and simplifies recovery. Second, centralize logs and audit data into a hardened Log Archive account and restrict access with SCPs and bucket policies. Third, use OUs to group accounts by policy needs — environment, regulatory boundary, or business unit — and attach SCPs at the OU level for consistent guardrails. Fourth, prefer AWS SSO for human access at scale and use cross-account roles selectively for automation or trusted delegation. Fifth, always test policies in a non-production OU before broad deployment and maintain a rollback path. Common mistakes include over-broad denies at Root, neglecting per-account budgets, and failing to route logs centrally. Finally, document ownership, billing, and incident response responsibilities for each account to avoid confusion during incidents. These practices keep your organization governable as it scales and reduce the chance of surprises. Let's summarize the three core ideas to carry forward. First, a multi-account strategy is about deliberate segmentation: define accounts by responsibility and trust boundary to reduce blast radius and simplify audits. Second, AWS Organizations provides the control plane: use the Root, Organizational Units, and Service Control Policies to centrally apply guardrails and consolidate billing. Remember that SCPs only restrict permissions; they do not grant them, and denies in SCPs override IAM grants. Third, design clear account roles: keep the management account for administration and billing, centralize logging in a hardened archive account, and separate security, shared services, development, production, and sandbox accounts. Combine consolidated billing with per-account budgets and tag-based reporting for accurate chargebacks.
